# A datetime literal with no offset, compiled and run as Go, then run again on
# the interpreter.
#
# The checker accepts `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM` with the seconds and the offset each
# optional (`checkStringReprLiteral`), and Go's emitted `mustParseDateTime`
# read RFC3339 alone -- which requires an offset. So the two most ordinary
# spellings of a datetime literal compiled fine and panicked the moment the
# program ran:
#
#     panic: parsing time "2024-01-15T10:30:00" as "2006-01-02T15:04:05Z07:00"
#
# A script rather than a golden, because the helper's text was never the
# question: it is one line either way and only running it says which.

sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

sngl test --platform=none app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

-- app.sngl --
import . "sngl:test"
import ui "sngl:ui"
import time "sngl:time"

component main ui.node {
    var minutes time.datetime = "2024-01-15T10:30"
    var seconds time.datetime = "2024-01-15T10:30:00"
    var offset time.datetime = "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z"
    var shown = ""

    effect(@mount {
        shown = string(seconds)
    })

    ui.text(value="{minutes}")
}

// Reaching the value at all is the assertion: each of the three spellings is
// parsed where the program starts, so a layout the helper does not know takes
// the whole run down before any test body is entered.
func testEveryLiteralSpellingSurvivesTheHelper(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.shown != "")
}

ui.window {
    main
}
-- testrun/bubbletea/go/app.sngl/main/1 --
sha256:20faf45f9bba2439f20cfcc6df239102
{
  "results": [
    {
      "Desc": "EveryLiteralSpellingSurvivesTheHelper",
      "Passed": true
    }
  ]
}
